{{Short description|Concept in category theory}}
In [[category theory]], an abstract branch of [[mathematics]], '''distributive laws''' between [[monad (category theory)|monad]]s are a way to express abstractly that two [[algebraic structure]]s [[distributive law|distribute]] one over the other.

Suppose that <math>(S, \mu^S, \eta^S)</math> and <math>(T, \mu^T, \eta^T)</math> are two monads on a [[category (mathematics)|category]] '''C'''.  In general, there is no natural monad structure on the composite [[functor]] ''ST''.  However, there is a natural monad structure on the functor ''ST'' if there is a distributive law of the monad ''S'' over the monad ''T''.

Formally, a '''distributive law''' of the monad ''S'' over the monad ''T'' is a [[natural transformation]]
:<math>l:TS\to ST</math>
such that the diagrams
:[[File:Distributive law monads mult1.svg|250px|Distributive law monads mult1]] &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [[File:Distributive law monads unit1.svg|200px|Distributive law monads unit1]]
:[[File:Distributive law monads mult2.svg|250px|Distributive law monads mult2]] &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [[File:Distributive law monads unit2.svg|200px|Distributive law monads unit2]]
[[commutative diagram|commute]].

This law induces a composite monad ''ST'' with
* as multiplication: <math>STST\xrightarrow{SlT}SSTT\xrightarrow{\mu^S\mu^T}ST</math>,
* as unit: <math>1\xrightarrow{\eta^S\eta^T}ST</math>.

== Examples ==

=== Monoids ===
Informally, one might say that the [[free monoid]] on a set is given by "the [[free semigroup]], plus an [[identity element]]". We can formalise this intuition, using the fact that both the free semigroup and the "free element" functors are monads.<ref name=":1"> {{cite book
 |author-link = Michael Barr (mathematician) |first1=Michael |last1=Barr |first2=Charles |last2=Wells
 |title       = Toposes, Triples and Theories
 |url         = http://www.case.edu/artsci/math/wells/pub/pdf/ttt.pdf
 |publisher   = [[Springer-Verlag]]
 |year        = 1985
 |isbn        = 0-387-96115-1
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20110514231306/http://www.case.edu/artsci/math/wells/pub/pdf/ttt.pdf
 |archive-date = 2011-05-14
}} </ref> Explicitly, consider the monads
:<math> T(X) := \sum_{n \ge 1} X^{n} </math>
:<math> S(X) := X+1 </math>,
(here addition denotes [[disjoint union]]), with unit maps given by:
:<math> \eta^{T}_{X} : X \to T(X) </math>
:<math> \eta^T_X(x) := x \in X^1 </math>

:<math> \eta^S_X : X \to S(X) </math>
:<math> \eta^S_X(x) := x \in X </math>.

The multiplication map <math> \mu^S_X : X+2 \to X+1</math> sends both elements of 2 to that of 1, but the multiplication on <math>T</math> is a bit more tricky to describe. First, note that an arbitrary element of <math>T(X)</math> is just a finite (nonempty) string of elements of <math>X</math>. The multiplication map <math> T^2(X) \to T(X) </math> should therefore take a string of words on <math>X</math> to one word. We choose <math> \mu^T_X(list) </math> to be the concatenation of all (finitely many) words in <math>list</math>.

What does a distributive law <math> l : TS \to ST </math> mean here? It takes a word on the set <math>X+1</math> to either a word on <math>X</math>, or the disjoint point in <math>1</math>. We choose the map that interprets the unit element <math>e \in 1</math> as the empty word; explicitly:
:<math> l(w) = w-e, </math>
where <math>w-e</math> is the word derived from <math>w</math> by removing all instances of <math>e</math>, unless <math>w</math> is all <math>e</math>'s, in which case it's defined to be <math>e \in 1</math>. The idea, in short, is this: if we view words on <math>X</math> as formal products of elements (i.e., the free semigroup operation), then <math>l</math> encodes that the freely added element <math>e</math> can be incorporated into the semigroup as a unit element (thereby making the structure into a monoid). Let us check that all the diagrams in the definition commute.

*<math> \mu^S_{T(X)} \circ S(l_X) \circ l_{S(X)} = l_X \circ T(\mu^S_X) </math>
::<math> LHS: w \mapsto (w-e') \mapsto (w-e'-e) \mapsto (w-e'-e) </math>
::<math> RHS: w \mapsto w[e/e'] \mapsto (w[e/e']-e) </math>,
<math>e,e'</math> being the elements of each copy of <math>1</math> in <math>X+1+1</math>, and where <math>w[e/e']</math> denotes the word <math>w</math> with every instance of <math>e'</math> replaced by <math>e</math>.
*<math> l_X \circ T(\eta^S_X) = \eta^S_{T(X)} </math>
::<math> LHS: w \mapsto w \mapsto w-e </math>
::<math> RHS: w \mapsto w </math>,
and note that for <math>w \in T(X)</math> we have <math>w-e = w</math>, as required.
*<math> S(\mu^T_X) \circ l_{T(X)} \circ T(l_X) = l_X \circ \mu^T_{S(X)} </math>
::<math> LHS: w \mapsto w[(v-e)/v] \mapsto w[(v-e)/v]-e \mapsto concat(w[(v-e)/v]-e) </math>
::<math> RHS: w \mapsto concat(w) \mapsto concat(w)-e </math>,
where: <math>concat(w)</math> is the concatenation of all words in <math>w</math>, i.e. the multiplication on <math>T</math>; and <math>w[(v-e)/v]</math> is the result of replacing every word <math>v</math> in <math>w</math> with <math>(v-e)</math>.
*<math> l_X \circ \eta^T_{S(X)} = S(\eta^T_X) </math>
::<math> LHS: (x \in X \ or \ e \in 1) \mapsto (x \ or \ e) \mapsto (x \ or \ e) - e </math>
::<math> RHS: (x \ or \ e) \mapsto (x \ or \ e) </math>.

In summary, the four commutation requirements encode the following ideas:
# "Deleting" elements <math>w-e'</math> behaves like replacing them with the identity, <math>w[e/e']</math>.
# Any word <math>w</math> on <math>X</math> doesn't contain the element <math>e</math>, so <math>w-e = w</math>. In other words, <math>X+1</math> truly is a disjoint union.
# In a list of words <math>w = (v_1,...,v_n)</math>, removing any instance of <math>e</math> in <math>v_i</math>, removing any remaining "empty word" <math>v_i = e</math>, and concatenating the resulting list, yields the same result as first concatenating <math>v_1v_2...v_n</math> then removing all instances of <math>e</math>.
# <math>x-e = x</math>, as already covered in 2; and <math>e-e = e</math>, meaning we should interpret <math>e</math> as the empty word.

=== Rings ===
This is the original example given by Beck,<ref name=":0" /> and is the motivation for the term "distributive law". Consider the two monads <math>G,M:\bold{Set} \to \bold{Set}</math> which send a set <math>X</math> to (the underlying set of) the [[Free group#Free abelian group | free commutative group]] and the [[free monoid]] on it, respectively. We shall regard the [[Formal group law|formal group]] operation as addition, and that of the monoid as multiplication. In this case, both composites <math> GM </math> and <math> MG </math> give the [[free ring]] functor. We can now use the fact that the free ring admits a distributive law <math> MG \to GM </math> to show that it's also a monad.

The distributive law of G over M means exactly that a product of sums (i.e. an element of <math> M(G(X)) </math>) can be identified with a sum of products (an element of <math> G(M(X)) </math>). Note that we say <math> G(X) </math>, the additive group, distributes over <math> M(X) </math>, the multiplicative monoid - contrary to the usual convention; see the next section.

== Terminology ==
The original description by Beck calls <math> l: TS \to ST </math> a distributive law ''of S over T''.<ref name=":0">{{cite book
 | first = Jon |last=Beck
 | author-link = Jonathan Mock Beck
 | year = 1969
 | contribution = Distributive laws
 | title = Seminar on Triples and Categorical Homology Theory, ETH 1966/67
 | series = Lecture Notes in Mathematics
 | volume = 80
 | pages = 119–140
 | doi = 10.1007/BFb0083084
 | isbn = 978-3-540-04601-1
 }}</ref> However, some authors prefer the reverse terminology, where <math> l </math> is instead said to be a distributive law ''of T over S''; this is because, arguably, the latter convention corresponds more closely to the usual distributive law between multiplication and addition - multiplication is typically said to distribute ''over addition'', by which one means that a ''product of sums'' can be rewritten as a ''sum of products'' <math> \prod \sum \to \sum \prod </math> (see [[Distributive_law_between_monads#Examples|Examples]]). Nevertheless, both terminologies are in use in different sources, and the original is what this article uses.<ref name=":2">{{nlab|id=distributive+law|title=Distributive law}}</ref>

== Related notions ==
=== BD-law ===
In the case where <math>T=S</math>, the distributive law map reduces to <math>K:T^2 \Rightarrow T^2</math>, and one may impose some additional conditions. <math>K</math> is called a '''BD-law''' on <math>T</math> if:
: '''''(D)''''' <math>K</math> is a distributive law, and
: '''''(B)''''' it satisfies the [[Yang-Baxter equation]]:
:: <math>K_{T(X)} \circ T(K_X) \circ K_{T(X)} = T(K_X) \circ K_{T(X)} \circ T(K_X)</math>
:: (as maps <math>T^3(X) \to T^3(X)</math>).

A ''BD-law'' is a '''BCD-law''' if the multiplication on <math>T</math> is "<math>K</math>-commutative", meaning that
: '''''(C)''''' <math>\mu^T_X \circ K_X = \mu^T_X</math>
:: (as maps <math>T^2(X) \to T(X)</math>).

Condition '''''(B)''''' is called a Yang-Baxter equation because it literally is the Yang-Baxter equation defined on [[monoid object]]s, when <math>T:\bold{C} \to \bold{C}</math> is viewed as a monoid in the category of [[endofunctor]]s on <math>\bold{C}</math>.<ref name=":4">{{Citation |title=Coalgebras, Braidings, and Distributive Laws |last=Kasangian |first=Stefano |date=2004-12-05 |work=Theory and Applications of Categories |volume=13 |pages=129-146 |url=https://www.emis.de/journals/TAC/volumes/13/8/13-08abs.html |url-status=live |publication-date=2004-11-08 |access-date=2025-09-04 |issn=1201-561X |last2=Lack |first2=Stephen |last3=Vitale |first3=Enrico M.}}</ref>

=== Entwining ===
For <math>P</math> an [[algebra over a field|algebra]] and <math>C</math> a [[coalgebra]] over a shared [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>k</math>, an '''entwining''' between them is a linear map <math>\psi:C \otimes P \to P \otimes C</math> satisfying analogous conditions to those that would be required, were <math>\psi</math> a distributive law. Specifically, the commutation diagram <math>CCP \to PC</math> that would be induced by a hypothetical multiplication <math>CC \to C</math> is replaced with one for <math>C \otimes P \to P \otimes C \otimes C</math> induced by the comultiplication <math>C \to C \otimes C</math>; likewise, the triangle diagram <math>P \to PC</math> is replaced with one of type <math>C \otimes P \to P \otimes k</math>, induced by the counit.<ref name=":3">{{cite journal |first1=T. |last1=Brzeziński |first2=S. |last2=Majid |title=Coalgebra Gauge Theory |journal=Comm. Math. Phys. |volume=191 |issue=2 |pages=467–492 |year=1998 |doi=10.1007/s002200050274 |arxiv=q-alg/9602022|bibcode=1998CMaPh.191..467B |s2cid=189829500 }}</ref>
